authorities.section: s0ma DSL — Language Specification & Coding Agent Rulebook

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use it for the strictness modes, which are the ratchet at the top of it rather than the ladder itself, and do not call one conversion a rung — converting a single module is one turn of rung three's loop.
concepts.plain_definition: The adoption ladder is the order the work is done in, and every rung is a place a project can honestly sit for weeks. Rung zero is reading: the codebase is scanned as it stands and comes back with the order to convert it in. Rung one sets the perimeter, which makes the tree a s0ma project without changing a line of it. Rung two is optional and marks up the existing Python where it lies, for a codebase too large to convert quickly. Rung three is the loop that converts one module at a time, leaves first, and is repeated until there is nothing left on the list. Rung four tightens the strictness mode as more of the project arrives. A project halfway up is a normal state with a number on it, not an unfinished mess.
concepts.purpose: Rewriting a working application in one go is the thing nobody can afford, so the alternative has to be a path with stopping places on it. Naming the rungs gives every stopping place a command that reaches it, a number that says it was reached, and one next step — which is what turns “we will adopt this eventually” into work somebody can pick up on a Tuesday and put down again on the Friday.
concepts.summary: The five-rung path a working Python codebase takes to become a s0ma application, one rung at a time.
concepts.use_when: Use adoption ladder for the whole ordered path, and rung for one place on it: which rung a project has reached, which rung a command belongs to, what the next rung asks for.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use it to argue that hand-written explanation is unwelcome. Guides are authored on purpose; the boundary governs only the factual claims inside them, which are checked against the system rather than trusted.
concepts.plain_definition: The authored-vs-generated boundary is the rule that every fact about the system has exactly one home. Facts a person states — what a part is for, what it promises, what it depends on — are authored, and are written once, in the source. Facts the build can work out for itself — which errors a piece of logic raises, which types it touches, what a finished documentation page says — are generated, and writing one of them by hand is refused rather than accepted as a shortcut. Documentation is rendered from the declarations; it is never maintained alongside them.
concepts.purpose: One home per fact is what makes disagreement impossible rather than merely unlikely. Where a fact is written in two places, one of them is eventually wrong and nothing can say which; where the generated half is rebuilt from the authored half every time, the two cannot part without the build seeing it.
concepts.summary: The line between what a person writes and what the build works out for itself, with no fact living on both sides of it.
concepts.use_when: Use this idea when deciding where a fact belongs: if a person has to state it, author it once; if the build can derive it, let the build derive it and never copy the answer anywhere.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not write an axon for something the build already works out for itself, such as which errors a part raises or which types it mentions; the language refuses those outright. Do not write two for one relationship either — one connection, one declaration.
concepts.plain_definition: An axon is a declared connection from one part of a system to another. It names the two ends, says what kind of dependence it is — one part calls another, builds it, reads settings from it, configures it, produces it, or consumes it — explains why the connection exists, says what travels along it, and records whether the two are tightly or loosely bound. A person writes it because it is a decision, not something a reader of the code could reliably work out.
concepts.purpose: It captures the architecture a codebase would otherwise only imply. Connections a machine can work out for itself — which errors a part may raise, which types it mentions — are worked out automatically and may never be written by hand, so an axon is reserved for the choices somebody made and the recorded graph is a record of decisions rather than a transcript of syntax.
concepts.summary: A written-down dependency between two parts: which one leans on which, why, and how tightly.
syntax: relation: <CALLS | CONSTRUCTS | READS | CONFIGURES | PRODUCES | CONSUMES>
concepts.use_when: Write an axon for a dependency that crosses a file boundary, where the build requires one, and for any dependency inside a single file that is architecturally significant enough that a reader should be told why it is there.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not hand-edit it. The build writes it and rewrites it on every build, so an edit is lost at best and misleading in the meantime; the source file is where a person writes, and this record is what the build made of what they wrote.
concepts.plain_definition: When the build turns a source file into Python it also writes a second file: a normalised record of everything that file declared, with every name in its full form, every shorthand expanded, every pattern resolved, every automatically-derived connection filled in, and a fingerprint of the whole. It says exactly what the source says, with none of the ambiguity, which is why it is the form tools and agents read.
concepts.purpose: It is the interface between a s0ma system and anything that wants to reason about it: a tool reading source has to parse a language, while a tool reading this record just reads structured data and every such tool sees the same picture. It also has room for honesty about what is not settled yet — a field can be recorded as deliberately absent, or as pending with a written reason, rather than simply being missing.
concepts.summary: The normalised record of one file's declarations that the build writes beside the code, for tools to read.
concepts.use_when: Read this record whenever a tool needs the structure of a system rather than its behaviour: building a reference page, answering a question about a part, or working out what a change would touch.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a cell for anything that computes, decides, fetches, or serves — that is a nerve, even when it is three lines long. A method that keeps a data structure internally consistent belongs on a cell; a method that acts on the system around it does not.
concepts.plain_definition: A cell is a part of a system that holds a shape or a value rather than doing work. Data models, configuration objects, fixed constants, enumerations, type names and error types are all cells. Like every other part it declares why it exists and what it represents, so a system can describe its own vocabulary and not only its own actions.
concepts.purpose: It draws the line between what a system is made of and what a system does. A tool asking what data a program handles reads the cells; a tool asking what a program does reads the nerves. Keeping structure out of the behaviour declarations is what makes both questions answerable at all.
concepts.summary: A declared piece of structure — a data shape, a fixed value, a setting, a type, or an error kind — rather than a piece of behaviour.
concepts.use_when: Use a cell for a data structure, a fixed value, a configuration object, an enumeration, a type name, or an error type. The test is whether the logic inside serves the data's own rules rather than the wider system's work.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not skip the check and go straight to a build hoping to save time. The check exists so that mistakes are found before anything is written, and the build runs the same validation anyway — so skipping it buys nothing and costs you the earlier, cheaper failure.
concepts.plain_definition: Working in this language is a short loop. You check the source, which validates everything and generates none of the build output — it keeps only one bookkeeping note of what it has already told you about — so it is cheap enough to run constantly. You build, which turns the source into ordinary Python together with the record of the system's own structure. You run the verifications. Then you ask the built system what it contains, which is how you confirm that the parts you meant to declare really are declared.
concepts.purpose: The loop is what keeps the description and the code in step. Because checking writes nothing it costs almost nothing to run, and because building produces the code and the record together the two cannot fall out of date with respect to each other.
concepts.summary: The everyday cycle: check the source, build it, run the verifications, then ask the system what it now contains.
concepts.use_when: Check constantly while writing, build when you want the output, verify before you share the change, and look at what the system now contains whenever you want to see what it believes about itself.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not put a contract on a structural part; a data shape says what it represents and what must always be true of it instead. Do not put one on a private helper either — helpers are scaffolding for the parts that carry contracts, and the check reports the fields when a helper carries them. And do not word a promise as a prohibition: what the part delivers belongs with what it guarantees, and only what it must never do, on any path, belongs in the third part.
concepts.plain_definition: A contract is the three-part agreement a working part carries: what must be true before it is called, what it guarantees once it has finished, and what it must never do, however it is called and whatever happens while it runs. All three are fields of the declaration, sitting alongside the reason the part exists, and a working part cannot be declared without them; when there is nothing to rule out, the third says so with the word none rather than being left off. Two related fields sit beside them — which errors the part may raise, and how long it may acceptably take. A watcher carries the third part as well: what it must never do while it watches.
concepts.purpose: It makes the agreement between caller and called a fact the system holds rather than something each reader reconstructs. A watcher can compare what actually happened against the promise, an agent can decide whether a part fits the situation in front of it — including what the part will never do — and a reviewer can see a promise or a prohibition change in a diff.
concepts.summary: What a working part needs before it runs, what it promises afterwards, and what it must never do, declared beside the code that has to keep all three.
syntax: expects: "<what must be true before it runs>"
guarantees: "<what is true once it has run>"
concepts.use_when: State all three parts on every working part: the condition a caller has to satisfy, the outcome the part will produce if that condition holds, and what it must never do, however it is called. When there is genuinely nothing to rule out, write none as the third part's answer.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a doc-guide for material that is purely a listing — a page assembled from the parts needs no author and is a doc-ref. Do not use one for conceptual writing that names no part of the system either; that is ordinary hand-written material, and this machinery would have nothing to check.
concepts.plain_definition: A doc-guide is a hand-written explanation — a walkthrough, a conceptual piece, a migration note — with one rule attached: wherever it names a part of the system it must do so through a marker the build resolves, embed a registered example, or state a claim the build can evaluate against what the system says about itself. Ordinary prose stays ordinary prose; it is the factual claims that are held to the system.
concepts.purpose: It is the concession that some things genuinely need explaining, made safe. Narrative usually rots because nothing checks it; here a guide that names a part which has since been renamed or removed fails the build, so the only claims that survive a merge are the true ones.
concepts.summary: A written guide whose every factual claim about a named part is checked against the system rather than trusted.
concepts.use_when: Use a doc-guide for task-oriented walkthroughs, conceptual explanations and migration notes that name real parts of the system.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a doc-ref where a reader has to be walked through something. It cannot hold narrative, and forcing one will produce a table where an explanation was needed; that is what a doc-guide is for.
concepts.plain_definition: A doc-ref is a declaration that produces a page of reference material by selecting parts of the system and printing named fields of each. It has no body and almost no writing: you say which parts it covers, which of their declared fields to show, and which file to write. Everything a reader sees comes from the parts themselves.
concepts.purpose: It removes the largest single source of stale documentation, the hand-written catalogue. A page assembled from the parts cannot describe a part that no longer exists, cannot miss one that was added, and cannot quote an old promise, because it holds a copy of none of that.
concepts.summary: A reference page assembled entirely from what the system already knows about itself, carrying no prose of its own.
concepts.use_when: Use a doc-ref for anything that is a list or a table of what the system contains: an interface reference, an error-code table, a catalogue of the parts in one layer.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Drift is not a word for a document that is badly written, out of date in its judgement, or missing a section. Those are editorial problems and a fingerprint cannot see them. Drift is the narrow, mechanical case where the source a document was built from has changed and the document has not been rebuilt.
concepts.plain_definition: Drift is what happens when a description and the thing it describes stop agreeing: the written record still says one thing while the code has quietly moved on. s0ma turns that disagreement into something a machine can notice. Every generated document carries a fingerprint of everything it was built from, and recomputing that fingerprint says at once whether the two still match.
concepts.purpose: Drift is the failure the whole product exists to prevent. Naming it, fingerprinting it, and rechecking it on every merge is what turns "the documentation is accurate" from a claim somebody makes into a fact the build can prove.
concepts.summary: The gap that opens when a written description and the thing it describes stop agreeing.
concepts.use_when: Ask for the drift check whenever you need to know whether the written record still matches the system: before a release, in the merge gate, and after any change to something a document describes.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use drift gate for the condition it detects — the divergence itself is drift — and do not use it for a check that only warns. A gate that does not refuse is not a gate.
concepts.plain_definition: The drift gate is where drift stops being a fact and becomes a failure. Every generated document carries a fingerprint of everything it was built from; the gate rebuilds the documents, compares the result with what is committed, and fails when the two differ. It runs in the same pipeline as the tests, so a change that leaves the written record behind cannot be merged, and the remedy is to rebuild rather than to remember.
concepts.purpose: Warnings get learned and then ignored. Making the disagreement a build failure — rather than a report somebody reads later, or never — is what turns an accurate written record from an intention into a property of the repository.
concepts.summary: The build step that refuses a change when the written record and the system it describes have parted.
concepts.use_when: Use drift gate for the enforcing step itself: the check that runs in the pipeline, compares what was built against what is committed, and refuses the change.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use embodiment for a system that merely talks to a device over a wire and declares nothing about it; that is an integration with no physical facts recorded. Never say the hardware is represented from outside the system: the whole point of the word is that the hardware is inside the boundary, declared like every other part.
concepts.plain_definition: Embodiment is what happens when the physical parts of a machine are declared as ordinary parts of the system that drives them, rather than described from outside it. A sensor or a motor is embodied when it is declared like everything else: an attached device is an integration, reading it or driving it is a nerve, its readings and physical value types are cells, and its physical facts — part identity, where it is mounted, size, mass, material, sweep, supply voltage, current draw — are recorded as declared metadata under one shared vocabulary. The language gains nothing new to make this possible.
concepts.purpose: Physical parts inside the boundary can be held to their declarations the way software is: a current ceiling the running machine exceeds becomes an anomaly the system raises about itself, and a physical fact that has changed becomes a discrepancy a build can find. Physical parts described from outside the boundary are a document, and documents drift.
concepts.summary: Bringing the physical parts of a machine inside the boundary of what a system knows about itself, as ordinary declared parts.
concepts.use_when: Use embodiment — and the word embodied — whenever physical parts are brought inside the self-knowing boundary as declared parts of the system, whether that is a sensor board, a drive train, or a door.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use an example as a substitute for a verification. Verifications exist to catch mistakes and may be as long and as thorough as they need to be; examples exist to be understood, and passing is a side effect of being honest rather than the point of the exercise.
concepts.plain_definition: An example is a small piece of code written to be read, declared as a part of the system in its own right. It says what it teaches, names the parts it demonstrates, and says where it runs. The build runs it, and an example that has stopped working fails the build exactly the way a broken verification does.
concepts.purpose: It closes the gap between sample code and real code. Because the example is registered against the parts it demonstrates, anyone editing one of those parts can ask which examples teach it and fix them in the same change — and because it executes, a demonstration that quietly stopped being true cannot survive.
concepts.summary: A short runnable demonstration, registered against the parts it teaches, that has to keep working.
concepts.use_when: Write an example when a reader needs to see a part in use, and keep it short: it will be read, and length is what makes a demonstration stop teaching.

concepts.do_not_use_when: The standard does not reach writing that names no part of the system. Conceptual and teaching material — the language specification among it — is hand-written and deliberately outside this machinery, because there is nothing in it for the build to check.
concepts.plain_definition: Executable evidence is the standard the documentation machinery holds every claim to. A statement about a named part of the system may exist in exactly three forms: printed from what that part declares, written as a claim the build evaluates against the system, or demonstrated by a registered example that is actually run. There is no fourth form, and a claim in none of the three is refused.
concepts.purpose: It makes documentation a projection of the system rather than a second description competing with it. A printed claim cannot be wrong, a checked claim fails loudly the moment it becomes wrong, and a demonstration that runs cannot quietly stop being true — so nothing survives on the strength of having once been correct.
concepts.summary: The rule that every factual claim in a document is printed from the system, checked against it, or demonstrated by code that runs.
concepts.use_when: Apply the standard whenever a document names a real part of the system: reach for a printed field first, a checked claim where a field alone will not say it, and a running demonstration where a reader needs to see the part in use.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not describe a feedback report as anonymous; it is pseudonymous and locally redacted, which is a different and more honest claim. Do not treat feedback as background collection either — nothing is gathered while you work, and nothing leaves the machine without a person approving that exact report.
concepts.plain_definition: Feedback is the path for telling the people who make s0ma what happened: a report prepared on your own machine, shown to you whole, and sent only after you have approved that exact report. Preparation is local and needs no network. The feedback data is redacted by a fixed rule and limited to an agreed list of context, so no transcripts, prompts, source, raw logs, or hardware identifiers travel by default. What you approved is what is transmitted, what is stored, and what the receipt refers back to.
concepts.purpose: Sending anything from a developer's machine is a trust decision, and the only honest way to ask for it is to show the whole feedback report first and let the person say no. Building it this way also keeps it harmless: nothing about preparing or sending a feedback report can change what a build, a check, or a running system does.
concepts.summary: A report to the people who make s0ma, shown to you in full and sent only after you approve that exact report.
concepts.use_when: Use the feedback path when something about s0ma itself is worth reporting — a diagnostic that confused you, a step that failed, a guide that misled you — and expect to read the report before it goes.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a ganglion to do the work it is watching; a watcher that also acts is two parts wearing one name. Do not use one to confirm a fixed expected result either — that is a verification, which runs on demand and either passes or fails, while a ganglion runs alongside the system and forms an opinion about it.
concepts.plain_definition: A ganglion is a part whose job is to watch other parts. It names which ones it observes — individually, or by a pattern covering a whole file or a whole layer — states what it expects normal behaviour to look like, says what should happen when what it sees does not match, and says what it must never do while it watches. It is the part of a s0ma system that forms judgements about the rest of it.
concepts.purpose: It is how a system notices its own trouble instead of waiting to be told about it. Because the watching relationship is declared, anyone can ask which parts of a system are watched, by what, and against which expectation — a question no ordinary monitoring setup can answer from the code.
concepts.summary: A declared watcher: it observes named parts of the system and judges what it sees against what it expected.
syntax: priors: "<what normal is expected to look like>"
on_anomaly: "<what to do when it is not>"
forbids: "<what it must never do while it watches>"
concepts.use_when: Use a ganglion when something has to assess behaviour rather than produce it: timing and promise-keeping at a single part, patterns across a file, or judgements that span the whole system.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a helper for anything another file needs; nothing outside the file can reach it and the build refuses the attempt. Do not use one for something with a real promise to keep either — the moment you want to say what it expects and guarantees, it is a nerve.
concepts.plain_definition: A helper is a function that exists to keep other declarations readable and never leaves the file it is written in. It declares why it exists and nothing else: no promises, no visibility setting, no dependency list, because the parts it serves are the ones that carry those. Other files cannot reach it and the system's list of components does not include it — though the file's own record still shows it, so nothing in a file is invisible.
concepts.purpose: It gives ordinary scaffolding a home. Without it a private twenty-line routine has to be either buried inside a larger part, where nobody can see it, or promoted to a full component with promises it does not deserve. The helper is the honest third answer, and it keeps the component list meaningful by keeping scaffolding out of it.
concepts.summary: A small private function inside one file, described but deliberately not registered as a part of the system.
concepts.use_when: Use a helper for a routine only this file calls and that carries no promise of its own: formatting, small shared setup, a recorder class several verifications reuse.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use an integration for a dependency inside your own program, and do not place one outside the infrastructure layer — talking to the outside world is an infrastructure job by definition, and the build refuses any other layer.
concepts.plain_definition: An integration is the declaration that describes a connection to something outside the program — a calendar service, a payment provider, a message queue. It names the part that builds the connection, the part that checks the connection is alive, and a short record of what the integration offers and what the environment has to supply, such as which settings must be present. From that declaration the build writes the routine wiring for you.
concepts.purpose: Every outside connection used to be assembled by hand in roughly the same shape, and hand-assembled shapes drift apart. Making it a declaration lets the build check the named pieces really exist, produce the same access points every time, and lets anyone ask what a system depends on beyond itself.
concepts.summary: A declared adapter to an outside system, naming how to build it, how to check it is alive, and what it needs to run.
concepts.use_when: Use an integration when your program talks to a service you do not control, and you want that fact, its readiness check and its requirements declared in one place.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not leave it to be inferred from a name, and do not use it to record how something works. The how belongs in the code and, where a promise is involved, in the contract fields beside it.
concepts.plain_definition: Intent is the sentence that says why a part exists. Every declared part carries one; no kind of code is exempt. It is not a comment and not a docstring bolted on afterwards — it is a field of the declaration, so it cannot be left out, cannot drift away from the code it belongs to, and travels with that code wherever the description is read.
concepts.purpose: It is the smallest unit of a system's self-knowledge and the one the rest depends on. Reference pages assembled from the parts, searches across a system, and an agent asking what something is for all read this field, which is why a system where every part states its reason can answer questions an ordinary codebase cannot.
concepts.summary: The declared reason a part exists, required on every part without exception.
concepts.use_when: Write an intent on every declaration, and write the reason rather than the mechanics — what the part is for, not a restatement of what its code does.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use interoception for structural facts, which hold whether or not anything is running, and do not use it as another word for monitoring: what distinguishes it is the comparison against what the part itself declared.
concepts.plain_definition: Interoception is the internal-state faculty of self-knowledge: the system's sense of how it is actually behaving compared with the behaviour it declared. A part can state what it expects of itself — how long a call should take, how often it may fail, how much memory or current it may draw — and the interoception verifier compares live measurements against those statements, so a part quietly running outside its own declared envelope becomes a reported fact instead of a surprise.
concepts.purpose: It gives the platform a second kind of truth to check. Structure can be verified from the code alone; behaviour can only be verified while the system runs, and without a name for that sense the runtime half of self-knowledge has nowhere to live.
concepts.summary: The runtime-state faculty: a system's sense of how it is behaving against how it said it would.
concepts.use_when: Use interoception when the sentence is about a running system measured against its own declarations: how fast, how often it fails, what it draws, and the anomalies raised when a reading crosses a declared bound.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not expect a kind on the declarations that have only one role. A verification, a private helper, a connection between parts and the three documentation declarations carry none, because there is nothing to choose between.
concepts.plain_definition: Every working part and every structural part declares a kind, which says which archetype it belongs to. A working part is a plain computation, a coordinator of other parts, an adapter to something outside, or a long-running service. A structural part is a data shape, a fixed value, a settings object, an enumeration, a type name, or an error type. Which kinds are available depends on what sort of declaration you are writing, and the build refuses a mismatch.
concepts.purpose: It lets a system group its own parts by role rather than by name. Asking for every adapter, or every fixed value, or every long-running service is a question the system answers directly — which is what makes a reference page assembled from the parts possible at all.
concepts.summary: The functional archetype of a part: what sort of working logic it is, or what sort of structure it holds.
syntax: kind: <MODEL | CONSTANT | CONFIG | ENUM | EXCEPTION | TYPE>
concepts.use_when: Choose a kind for every working part and every structural part, picking the archetype that describes what it is rather than what it happens to be called.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not mix layers within one file; the language requires them to match exactly. And when two files in different bands need to share something, do not reach across: move the shared thing down into a band both can reach, or have the lower band publish an interface the higher one fills in.
concepts.plain_definition: Every s0ma file declares one layer and every part inside the file shares it. The five bands are the subject matter itself, the work that coordinates it, the two edges where a program meets people and meets other systems, and the band s0ma keeps for its own machinery. A fixed table says which band may reach which: the subject matter reaches only itself and the framework, the two edges reach inward but never each other, and nothing reaches outward.
concepts.purpose: It stops a codebase turning into a web where anything may call anything. Because the band is declared and the reachable pairs are fixed, an accidental dependency from the subject matter out to a screen or a database is refused at build time rather than discovered years later.
concepts.summary: The architectural band a file and everything in it belongs to, and the rule about which bands may depend on which.
concepts.use_when: Choose the layer when you create a file, and choose it for the file rather than for one part — the layer applies to everything the file contains.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use metacognition for the act of recording structure or measuring behaviour — those are the other two faculties, and this is what is done with what they record. Do not let it imply a language model is involved: the reasoning here is rule-based by principle, so that a system can answer for itself with no network and no model call.
concepts.plain_definition: Metacognition is the reasoning faculty of self-knowledge: answering questions about the system by reasoning over its recorded model instead of re-reading its source. Asking what would break if this changed, asking where a new part belongs, asking a question in plain words, and noticing that the model and the code no longer agree are all metacognition. Each takes the recorded model as its subject, and each follows fixed rules rather than calling a language model, so the answers are reproducible and available offline.
concepts.purpose: It is what makes the record worth keeping. A record nobody can question is an archive; a record that answers what would break if this changed, and where a new part belongs, is the reason the other two faculties are maintained at all.
concepts.summary: The reasoning faculty: answering questions by working over the system's own model rather than over its code.
concepts.use_when: Use metacognition when the sentence is about reasoning over the recorded model: queries, impact analysis, guidance about where something belongs, and the detection of disagreement between the model and reality.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not call a document a mirror when it is edited in its own right, or when it merely covers the same ground as another. That is a second document, and two documents describing one thing are how a contradiction gets shipped.
concepts.plain_definition: A mirror is a second copy of a document, committed at another path because something genuinely needs it there — most often inside an installed package, so an agent working on a project can read the guides without a copy of the repository. A mirror is never edited in place: it is copied from the one source, and a check compares the two character for character and fails the build when they have parted. The source is the document; the mirror is a delivery of it.
concepts.purpose: Some documents really do have to exist in two places, and the honest way to allow that is to make the second copy mechanically dependent on the first. A copy nobody compares becomes a second source of truth within a week; a copy compared on every build stays a delivery mechanism.
concepts.summary: A committed copy of a document, held identical to its one source by a check that fails when they part.
concepts.use_when: Use mirror for a committed copy whose whole job is to be identical to a source elsewhere in the repository, and name the source whenever you name a mirror.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use the header to describe a single function or value; that belongs to the declaration for that part. And do not list a name among the published parts unless the part itself is marked public — the header and the part have to agree about what other files may reach.
concepts.plain_definition: A module declaration is the first thing in a s0ma source file and it speaks for the whole file: it gives the file a name, places it in one architectural band, states what the file is responsible for, and lists both the outside code it draws on and the parts of itself it lets other files use. Nothing enters or leaves the file without appearing in one of those lists.
concepts.purpose: It makes a file's dependencies a declared fact instead of a scatter of import lines. Because the header is the only door in and out, a tool can answer what a file needs and what it offers by reading one block, and the build can refuse a file that reaches for something it never declared.
concepts.summary: The header every s0ma source file opens with, naming the file and declaring everything that enters and leaves it.
syntax: intent: "<what this module is responsible for>"
concepts.use_when: Write one at the top of every s0ma file, before any other declaration. There is no such thing as a s0ma file without one.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a nerve for something that only holds a shape or a value — a fixed value, a data structure, or a type belongs in a cell. Do not use one for the part that watches other parts and draws conclusions about them; that is a ganglion. And do not use one for a small private routine nobody outside the file calls; that is a helper.
concepts.plain_definition: A nerve is a piece of working logic that carries a description of itself. You write the function — or, for a long-running service, the class — as you normally would, and above it you state what it is for, what it needs from its caller, what it promises in return, and what it must never do. Those statements are part of the declaration rather than a comment beside it, so they travel with the code from then on.
concepts.purpose: Nerves are how a s0ma system knows what its own moving parts do. Because the description is declared rather than remembered, the system can be asked what it contains and answer from the code itself, instead of from a document somebody hopefully kept up to date.
concepts.summary: A piece of working logic that carries its own account of what it does, what it needs, and what it promises.
concepts.use_when: Use a nerve for anything that acts: a step that computes, decides, fetches, or serves. If you would reach for a function or a service class, reach for a nerve.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use it for the conversion work inside it: a file joins the self-model by being converted, not by the perimeter moving. A file named as an entry point or a package marker sits outside the account rather than inside it, so setting a perimeter is never a claim that the code within it has been converted.
concepts.plain_definition: The perimeter is four settings a project keeps in its own pyproject.toml: where its source lives, which files are the plain-Python entry points, which files are package markers that only re-export, and which strictness mode it is held to. Together they say what s0ma is answerable for here. Anything inside the perimeter that has not been converted yet is reported as unknown, which is the honest list of what is left to do; anything named as an entry point or a package marker is reported as exempt, by name, so what sits outside is something a reader can check rather than something they have to trust.
concepts.purpose: A project that adopts s0ma a piece at a time needs a way of saying “this much, so far” that is exact enough to check. Without a declared perimeter the toolchain would have to guess which plain Python was left over and which was meant to stay plain, and a guess is the one thing an account of a system may not rest on.
concepts.summary: The line a project draws around the code s0ma answers for, and the files it deliberately leaves outside.
concepts.use_when: Use perimeter for the declared boundary itself: setting it on an existing tree, widening it as more is converted, or reading what it leaves outside.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use proprioception for how a system is behaving while it runs — that is interoception — and do not use it as another word for the whole of self-knowledge. It carried that larger meaning before the three faculties were named separately, and it no longer does.
concepts.plain_definition: Proprioception is the structural faculty of self-knowledge: the system's sense of its own composition — which parts exist, what each is for, which layer it belongs to, and what depends on what. It is carried by the index every part must enter in order to exist, the verifier that compares that index against the code, the map of dependencies, the layer rules, and the relationships recorded in the build's machine-readable output.
concepts.purpose: It names the sense most of the platform serves today and keeps it separate from the other two, so that a claim about structure is not read as a claim about behaviour. A system with proprioception can answer what would break if this changed without anybody reading the code.
concepts.summary: The structural faculty: a system's sense of what it is made of and how it is wired together.
concepts.use_when: Use proprioception when the sentence is about structure: what exists, what it is called, where it sits, and what it depends on.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not read presence in the index as permission to call something. The index answers what exists and what may be observed; what may be called across files is the separate question the publish list and the visibility setting answer.
concepts.plain_definition: When a s0ma system starts, every declared part registers itself in one index under a full name that joins the file's name and the part's own. Because the name is qualified, two files may each contain a part called the same thing without either shadowing the other. The index is what the system consults when anything asks what it contains, and it is complete — it includes the parts no other file is allowed to call.
concepts.purpose: It makes self-knowledge a running fact rather than only a build-time one. The watchers, the verifications and the documentation machinery all resolve names against this index rather than against the shorter list of what a file publishes, which is how a system can describe every part of itself while keeping most of them private to call.
concepts.summary: The live index of every part in a running system, each held under the full name that joins its file and itself.
concepts.use_when: Reach for the index when you want to know what a running system actually contains, as opposed to what one file publishes to its neighbours.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not call a page a release build when it came from an untagged state, however finished the work feels, and do not use historical as a polite way of keeping a page that is simply wrong. A page that has been superseded points at what replaced it.
concepts.plain_definition: A release channel is the label every rendered page carries saying which build it came from and how far it can be trusted. Release means the page was built from the exact state of a tagged version and describes that version and no other. Preview means it was built from the moving main line, so it may describe work that has not shipped, and every preview page says so where a reader can see it. Historical means the page describes a version that has passed, kept for the people still on it and never presented as current.
concepts.purpose: A reader arriving from a search engine cannot tell which version a page describes, and a page that is right about tomorrow is wrong today. Stamping the channel onto the page itself makes that question answerable without anyone having to ask.
concepts.summary: Which build a page came from — a released version, a preview of work in progress, or a record kept for a version that has passed.
concepts.use_when: Use the channel words whenever a document's currency is at stake: saying which build a page came from, deciding whether unreleased work may appear in it, or marking material that has been superseded.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use it for parts of your own project written in this language; those belong in the uses list. And do not expect these names in the declaration fields themselves — those fields may only name things the system is able to describe.
concepts.plain_definition: The requires list names the outside code a file needs: standard library modules, installed packages, and specific names from either. The build turns each entry into the right import line. Sibling lists cover the variations — one for packages that may not be installed, one for imports a running system supplies in a way no checker can see, and one for imports deferred until the moment they are first used.
concepts.purpose: It puts outside dependencies in the same declared place as everything else, so a file's needs can be read in one block instead of searched for. It also lets the build confirm that what a file claims to need is really installed, and say so when a file claims something it never uses.
concepts.summary: The module header's list of code from outside the project — the ordinary Python imports, declared.
syntax: soft_requires: [<packages that may not be installed>]
concepts.use_when: List an entry for every outside module or name the file's code refers to, and choose the sibling list that matches how the dependency should fail: quietly absent, invisible to the checker, or deferred to the first call.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use s0ma for a single package: the runtime is s0ma-core, the language is s0ma-dsl, the authoring interface is s0ma-mcp, and the viewer is s0ma-studi0. Do not use it for something somebody built on the platform either — that is a s0ma project. And it is always written with a digit zero.
concepts.plain_definition: s0ma is a Python platform built on one idea — that a system should carry an accurate, queryable, machine-readable model of itself, and that the model should be load-bearing rather than descriptive. Four layers deliver it: a runtime that records and verifies the parts of a running system, a language and compiler that refuse to build undeclared or undescribed code, an interface that lets a coding agent author against the same rules, and a viewer that draws what the model says. One version, one philosophy, four packages.
concepts.purpose: It exists because the written account of a system and the system itself part company within weeks, and nobody can tell which half is lying. s0ma removes the parallel account: the description is rendered from declarations the system needs in order to run at all, so a description that has gone wrong is a system that refuses to start.
concepts.summary: The platform built on one idea: software should carry an accurate, queryable model of itself.
concepts.use_when: Use s0ma for the platform as a whole — the four packages, the language, and the idea they serve — and use the specific package name when you mean one of them.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not leave code in a file outside a declaration, and do not use the three-hyphen line anywhere but between a declaration's description and its code. The two declarations that carry no code — a connection between parts and the module header — leave the separator out entirely.
concepts.plain_definition: A s0ma source file has a fixed anatomy. It opens with the module header that speaks for the whole file, then carries one or more declarations, and every piece of code in it belongs to exactly one of them — the language refuses a block that belongs to none. Inside a declaration the description comes first and the code comes after, with a line of exactly three hyphens at the left margin between them.
concepts.purpose: The fixed shape is what lets both people and machines read a file with no guesswork: the header always says what the file is, the description always comes before the code it describes, and the separator always marks where one stops and the other starts. Nothing about a file's meaning depends on convention or on where a reader happens to look.
concepts.summary: One source file: a module header first, then declarations, each separated from its code by a line of three hyphens.
syntax: intent: "<what this module is responsible for>"
# then one or more declarations, in any order:
concepts.use_when: Every file you write in this language has this shape; there is no other arrangement to choose between.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use self-knowledge where one faculty is meant; the specific words exist and say more. Do not use it for the record itself either: the artifact is the self-model, and self-knowledge is what having one lets a system do.
concepts.plain_definition: Self-knowledge is a system's ability to maintain an accurate, queryable, machine-readable model of itself: its structure, its behaviour while it runs, and the reasoning that can be done over both. It is the umbrella term, and it spans three faculties that answer different questions — proprioception asks what the system is made of, interoception asks how it is behaving against what it declared, and metacognition reasons over the model itself.
concepts.purpose: The word gives the product one name for the whole capability, so that the three faculties can be discussed separately without any one of them being mistaken for the entire idea. Before it, the structural third carried the name of the whole, which quietly hid the other two.
concepts.summary: The umbrella faculty: a system's ability to hold an accurate, queryable model of itself.
concepts.use_when: Use self-knowledge whenever the whole capability is meant, or when the particular faculty does not matter to the sentence.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use self-model for the capability of having one; that is self-knowledge. Do not use it for a diagram or a written page produced from it either — those are views of the model, and the model is what they are views of.
concepts.plain_definition: The self-model is the system's record of itself: every declared part with its purpose, its kind, its layer, what it promises and what it depends on, together with the relationships between the parts and the documentation and examples attached to each. It is load-bearing rather than descriptive — being declared is a condition of a part existing at all, so the record cannot be skipped without the system failing to start.
concepts.purpose: Making the record load-bearing is what stops it rotting. A description kept beside the code is optional, and optional records go stale; a record the system needs in order to run is maintained by everyone who touches the code, whether or not they were thinking about documentation at the time.
concepts.summary: The queryable record of a system's parts, their relationships, and the documentation and examples attached to them.
concepts.use_when: Use self-model for the recorded artifact itself — the thing that is queried, rendered, verified, and compared against reality.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not reach for a forgiving mode to get a release out. The extra release requirements are the ones that keep a published system honest, and turning them off does not make the problems they name go away.
concepts.plain_definition: A strictness mode decides whether a finding is a warning or a refusal. The most forgiving mode exists for bringing an existing codebase across, where nearly everything is a warning. The everyday mode is balanced. The strict mode makes nearly everything a refusal and is meant for automated checks before a merge. The release mode adds requirements of its own: every public working part verified or explicitly claimed as covered elsewhere, every file carrying a real version, and every cross-file connection explained in a person's own words.
concepts.purpose: It lets one set of rules serve a codebase at every stage of its life. Silence would be the wrong default in a system built on explicitness, so nothing is ever ignored; what changes is whether a finding stops you now or is recorded for later.
concepts.summary: How severely the build treats its own findings, from forgiving during adoption to unforgiving before a release.
concepts.use_when: Use the forgiving mode while adopting the language, the balanced one day to day, the strict one in the automated checks before merging, and the release one when shipping. Which mode applies is decided in this order: the `--mode` flag on the command, else the project's `mode` setting in `pyproject.toml`, else the command's own default, which is `strict` for `s0ma check` and `dev` for the rest.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use a test to show how something is used — a reader learns from an example, which is written to be read, while a test is written to catch mistakes. Do not use one where the real verification lives in an outside suite either; say so in the part's own coverage claim instead.
concepts.plain_definition: A test in s0ma is a declaration like any other. It says what behaviour it verifies and, crucially, names the parts it is verifying, so the link between a check and the thing checked is recorded rather than guessed from a file name. The build turns it into an ordinary runnable test, and the system can be asked which of its parts are covered and by what.
concepts.purpose: It turns coverage from a number into a structure. Because each test names its targets, a system can list the public parts nobody verifies, and the strictest mode refuses a release while any public working part has neither a test nor a written claim that an outside suite covers it.
concepts.summary: A verification written as a declared part of the system, naming exactly which parts it checks.
concepts.use_when: Write a test declaration for behaviour you want verified inside the language, where the coverage should become part of the system's own record of itself.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not use it for code from outside the project; that is the requires list. And do not leave an entry in place once nothing in the file refers to it — an unused entry is reported, because a declared dependency nobody exercises is a claim that is no longer true.
concepts.plain_definition: The uses list names every part in another s0ma file that this file refers to — whether it calls it, builds it, raises it, or merely names it in a type. Each entry has to be something the other file has published, and each has to satisfy the layer rule, so a file's reach across the project is a declared and checked list rather than a set of import lines nobody audits.
concepts.purpose: It turns the dependency graph between files into a declared fact. Because it covers every kind of reference and not only calls, the recorded graph is complete — which is what makes it safe to ask what a change to one file would affect.
concepts.summary: The module header's list of parts in other s0ma files that this file is allowed to reach.
concepts.use_when: Add an entry whenever this file refers to something in another s0ma file, by any means at all.

concepts.do_not_use_when: Do not mark something public purely so a verification can reach it; that is exactly the workaround the third setting exists to retire. And do not read internal as hidden — an internal part is fully visible to watchers, verifications, and anything asking the system what it contains.
concepts.plain_definition: Every working and structural part declares a visibility. Public means other files may use it, provided the module header lists it too. Internal means only the file it lives in may call it. The third setting opens a part to verification code anywhere in the project without putting it on the public surface. Visibility governs calling and nothing else: watchers, verifications and the documentation machinery reach every part regardless, because a system that cannot see all of itself cannot describe itself.
concepts.purpose: It separates two questions that are usually tangled: who may depend on this, and who may look at it. Making the first restrictive and the second total is what lets a s0ma system keep a small public surface and a complete self-description at the same time.
concepts.summary: Who may call a part from another file: everyone, nobody, or verification code only.
concepts.use_when: Mark a part public when other files are meant to use it, internal when it is an implementation detail, and use the third setting for a detail that verification code genuinely has to exercise directly.

journeys.intent: Meet the two refusals a working project runs into — a file the toolchain owns that somebody edited, and a promise left unwritten before a release — and get back to a clean run from each without guessing.

recovery_paths.action: Two honest answers and no third: move the hand-written change into the source it belongs in and build again, or accept losing it and build with --force. The build stops until you pick one, because the two copies cannot both be right.

Ask for the health report first: it says which s0ma packages this machine actually has and what this project is set to, which is what the warning is about. Then name s0ma-core and s0ma-dsl in the project's own list of dependencies.

Write the value the field is waiting for and ask again, or leave the note where it is and stop asking for the release reading until you are ready. A written-down debt is allowed; it earns nothing, and it will not let a release through.

steps.expected_outcome: One line saying how many files were read and that nothing in them was refused.
steps.purpose: Ask whether the project holds together, so that everything after this is measured against a run that was clean.

steps.expected_outcome: The build stops, names the file and the failure, and writes nothing — so the hand-written line is still there to read.
steps.purpose: Build again once a line has been added by hand to a file under build, which is a folder the toolchain writes and owns.

steps.expected_outcome: A clean build, and the file back to what the source says it should be — the hand-written line gone, as asked.
steps.purpose: Say out loud which of the two copies survives: rebuild from the written source and let the hand-written line go.

steps.expected_outcome: The finding that was a warning a moment ago is now the reason the run fails, and the last line names the reading you got.
steps.purpose: Ask the same question at release strictness, once a promise in the source has deliberately been left unwritten.

steps.expected_outcome: The clean line again, this time earned under the reading that refuses a debt.
steps.purpose: Write the promise the field was waiting for and ask once more, at the strictness a release has to pass.

steps.expected_outcome: What is installed, what this project is set to, whether the build is fresh, and one thing to do next.
steps.purpose: When you cannot tell which of these you are in, ask for the health report before changing anything.

journeys.intent: Write your first module into a project that already builds, and follow it through to the point where the system can describe it back to you.

recovery_paths.action: The check stopped on the code under one of your declarations and named the file and the line it stopped at. Repair that line, then ask the same question again — nothing is built from a file the toolchain cannot read.

steps.expected_outcome: A clean run says how many files it read and that it found nothing wrong. Anything it is unhappy about is listed with the file and the line that caused it.
steps.purpose: Ask whether the module you have just written holds together, before anything is built from it.

steps.expected_outcome: One line per module built and one line per file written, ending with the count of modules and where the manifest went. Your new module appears among them.
steps.purpose: Turn the source into ordinary Python, and write the record of what each file declared beside it.

steps.expected_outcome: The module's own header, then every part it holds with who may call it and what archetype it is, then the connections the build worked out for itself, then what the file publishes.
steps.purpose: Ask the built module what it now contains, and read back the parts you declared.

journeys.intent: Go from an installed toolchain to a project that checks clean, builds, and can tell you what it contains — a first session with s0ma, start to finish.

recovery_paths.action: Your file asked for something this environment cannot import. Ask for the health report: it says which s0ma packages are installed here and whether it can see your project at all, which is the question a missing import raises. If something is genuinely absent, install it again by the route you first used.

The check stopped before it could read the file and named it, along with the value it would not accept. Repair that value in the source you wrote and ask the same question again — nothing is built from a file the toolchain cannot read, so there is nothing else to undo.

steps.expected_outcome: A new folder, each file named as it is written, and a note that the first build has already run.
steps.purpose: Turn an empty folder into a project: source you can read, a starter feature, and a first build, from one command.

steps.expected_outcome: One line saying how many files were read and that nothing in them was refused.
steps.purpose: Ask the toolchain whether what is in the project holds together, before anything is built from it.

steps.expected_outcome: A new file in the folder you chose, and a line saying the file it has just written is already valid.
steps.purpose: Add a module of your own, so that the project holds something you wrote rather than only what came with it.

steps.expected_outcome: The same clean line with one more file counted — or the file, and the value it could not accept, quoted back at you.
steps.purpose: Say what your module is for in the places the file leaves for it, then ask the same question again.

steps.expected_outcome: How many modules were written, where they went, and the name of the list that accounts for them.
steps.purpose: Turn the source you have just checked into ordinary Python, next to the record of what the project contains.

steps.expected_outcome: Every module with its band, its purpose and the parts inside it, the one you wrote among them.
steps.purpose: Ask the project what it now knows about itself, and read your own sentence back out of it.

steps.expected_outcome: The number of nodes the graph holds, and how many connections have been declared between them — none, so far.
steps.purpose: Look at how the pieces are wired to one another, which in a project this young is mostly a count.

journeys.intent: Let a coding agent take a project from first sight to a built component and back out again without ever leaving its own tool channel: ask the tree what it is, write a component from its intent, have the toolchain check it, build, then read the result back out of the self-model rather than out of the code.

recovery_paths.action: The check refuses the edited component because its provides: list names an operation the body never defines. Add the missing def, or take the name out of provides:, and walk the loop the fix_check_failures prompt lays out until the check is clean.

The body carries its own import line, and the build writes imports from the declarations instead. Move it into the module header — requires: for Python, uses: for another s0ma component — take the line out of the body, and ask the check again.

The build refuses because generated code was edited by hand, and that edit would be silently overwritten. Move the change back into the .s0ma source it belongs to, undo the hand edit, and ask the check again before building.

steps.expected_outcome: One answer with the whole posture in it: whether this is a s0ma project at all, which mode it is in, every module it already holds and whether each is still fresh, what is built, the short list of rules worth following here, and a named next call. A directory that is not a project is a valid answer, not an error.
steps.purpose: Find out what this tree already is before writing anything into it.

steps.expected_outcome: A new .s0ma source written into the project and handed back in full, already checked on its own and already valid, so the intent and the contracts can be edited straight away rather than guessed at.
steps.purpose: Start the new behaviour from its intent, in a skeleton the toolchain already accepts.

steps.expected_outcome: Either a clean answer counting the files it read, or findings that each name the file, the line, the failure and what to do about it — and whether the problem is new since the last green build or was here before this session.
steps.purpose: Ask whether what was just written holds together, before anything is built from it.

steps.expected_outcome: The generated code and a manifest naming every module and the order they import in, written once and the same every time — plus whatever the build still wants, which in a fresh project includes a warning that the s0ma runtime it now imports has not been declared as a dependency.
steps.purpose: Turn the checked sources into the artifacts the project runs from.

steps.expected_outcome: The component's own record: its canonical name, what kind of part it is, who may call it, the intent and the contracts it was authored with, and what it provides — what the system knows about itself rather than a reading of the code it emitted.
steps.purpose: Read back what the build now knows about the component, instead of reading the code it wrote.

journeys.intent: Take a Python application that already works and walk it up the adoption ladder: read what is there without changing a line of it, set the perimeter, write down what a module promises, convert that module, and prove the promise survived.

recovery_paths.action: At the perimeter this is the true reading, not a fault: nothing has been converted yet, so the self-model has nothing to answer with. It is the number the work exists to move. steps.expected_outcome: One screen: what was found, the perimeter it would declare, the first ten modules of a leaves-first conversion order with a proposed layer each, anything worth knowing about the imports, and the next command to run.
steps.purpose: Read the whole codebase without changing any of it, and get back the order to convert it in.

steps.expected_outcome: Exactly two things written and both quoted back at you: a [tool.s0ma] table appended to the pyproject.toml you already had, and one marked block added to AGENTS.md. No application file is touched, and --dry-run prints the same thing and writes nothing.

steps.expected_outcome: The versions installed here, the project root and the strictness mode it is in, and one finding saying nothing has been built yet — which is the truth at the perimeter.
steps.purpose: Ask whether the toolchain and the project now agree that this is a project at all.

steps.expected_outcome: One line per file: the entry point and the package marker recognised by name and by the setting that exempted them, every application file listed as UNKNOWN, and the counts underneath.
steps.purpose: Read back the honest backlog — every file that is neither converted nor declared as deliberately exempt.

steps.expected_outcome: Nought per cent for structure, which is correct on the first day, the strictness mode you are in, and the exempt files listed by name so what sits outside s0ma is a reading rather than a matter of trust.
steps.purpose: Turn the same facts into one number, so that the work has something to move.

steps.expected_outcome: One committed file at the project root, adopt-baseline.s0ma.json, holding what that module's Python offers its callers today: every public name, how each one is called, the type each one declares, what each one says about itself. The closing message says where the record is and asks you to commit it, because once the Python file is gone it cannot be taken again.
steps.purpose: Write down what the module promises, while the Python that promises it is still there to read.

steps.expected_outcome: One new file beside the module it came from, and a count of the work left in it: the structure is derived from your Python and every field that says what something is for arrives as a line for you to write. The Python file is read and not changed — it is still the code that runs — and because the baseline is already taken, the closing message names one command after this one rather than two.
steps.purpose: Take the first module on that order and turn it into a draft you can finish.

steps.expected_outcome: One line per module saying the surface is the same, or one line per difference: the name it is about, what moved in plain words, and the text before and after. What the build adds around your code — the registration, the generated header and import block, the order of __all__ — is not a difference. It exits non-zero on any finding, writes nothing anywhere, and ends by sending you to the project's own tests, which are the check it stands in for — and, while the Python file is still there, by printing the three things that finish the conversion: the lines that bind the module's old name to the built one, computed for this project's own layout, that the s0ma runtime has to be declared and installed, and that the build directory ships with the application from now on.
steps.purpose: Ask whether the module s0ma built still promises what the Python promised, before anything is deleted.

steps.expected_outcome: One screen, for somebody who has not read any of this: which rung of the ladder the project is on in plain words, how many of its modules are converted, half drafted, registered where they stand or still plain Python, how many baselines have been taken and what the comparison says about what has been built, which module is part way through, and one command to run next. Where more than one module is half converted the step is for the one furthest along, because finishing what is started beats starting another. It writes nothing.
steps.purpose: Come back to a retrofit that is only part way up the ladder and find out where it stands and what to do next.
